Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: Mary, a 58-year-old North American widow, has been living with the aftermath of a traumatic event that occurred several years ago. On the day in question, she had gone to pick up her husband from work and was met by emergency responders who were attending to an accident involving his vehicle. The scene was chaotic and filled with the acrid smell of burning rubber and gasoline, which lingered long after the paramedics left. Since then, Mary has been struggling with a myriad of symptoms that have significantly impacted her daily life. Every year on the anniversary of the event, she finds herself unable to avoid intrusive thoughts and vivid flashbacks that are often triggered by these same odors. The sight of ambulances driving past her house or hearing sirens in the distance brings back intense feelings of panic and fear. She is also acutely aware of car accidents happening on the news or even in real-time, as these images serve to remind her of the day her life changed. Mary’s sense of safety has been severely compromised. Unexpected movements nearby cause her to react as if she were still in danger, jumping at sudden noises and feeling an overwhelming urge to flee. This hypervigilance is particularly acute during the night when her sleep is often disrupted by these startle responses. Despite her efforts to wind down before bed, Mary frequently finds herself awake long into the night, her mind racing with memories of that fateful day. To cope with this heightened sense of danger, Mary has developed a ritual of repeatedly checking that all doors and windows are locked before she can even begin to feel secure in her home. This compulsive behavior has become increasingly time-consuming and intrusive, often leaving her feeling exhausted and frustrated by the end of each day. Mary’s memories of the event fluctuate wildly between vivid and hazy. When she deliberately tries to recall what happened, she finds it extremely difficult to access those memories clearly; yet, when triggered unexpectedly by something in her surroundings, she is overwhelmed with a flood of sensory details that feels as if she were reliving the moment all over again. The smell of burning rubber can instantly transport her back to that tragic day, leaving her feeling lost and disoriented. Over time, these symptoms have taken a toll on Mary’s daily life. She has grown increasingly isolated, avoiding public places or any situation where she might encounter ambulances or news reports about car accidents. Her once-active social life has dwindled as she struggles to engage with others without being constantly on edge. Despite her best efforts to manage these symptoms on her own, the intensity of Mary’s reactions and the frequency of her triggers have become overwhelming. What finally brought her to seek help was a particularly harrowing episode during one of those anniversaries, where she found herself unable to leave her home for days due to intense panic attacks. Mary is now in a place where she recognizes that things need to change. She is most afraid of continuing this cycle of avoidance and isolation, which has left her feeling trapped and helpless. At the same time, she is hoping for some relief from these overwhelming memories and fears, and a return to a sense of peace and normalcy in her daily life. As Mary begins therapy, it becomes clear that her symptoms are deeply intertwined with her experiences following her husband’s accident. The anniversary of the event, emergency contexts, and crash imagery serve as potent reminders of her trauma, each evoking powerful emotional responses that challenge her ability to feel safe and secure. Her persistent efforts to avoid triggers and maintain a sense of control through compulsive behaviors highlight the significant impact this trauma has had on her life. Mary’s journey towards healing will involve addressing these specific triggers, challenging her negative appraisals about safety and threat, and developing coping strategies that allow her to navigate her daily life with greater ease. With support and guidance, Mary is hopeful that she can find a way to reclaim her sense of self and regain control over the memories that have long held her captive.
